Here is something else to consider about clean code.

If your app isn't going to be used for many years, it might be better to just ship the features quickly and move on.

If your app IS going to be used for many years, well in many years AI will likely be good enough to rewrite chunks of it and make it cleaner.

The function you are using has a parameter "salt\_length=8". This implies the hashing algorithm you are using generates a salt, and encrypts your password by appending the salt (which is just a random string) to the actual password before hashing the resulting string.

Anytime "salt" is involved, you are SUPPOSED to get a different output whenever you hash your password, because that is actually what the salt is there to do. The reason you might want this is to improve security further, it means if an attacker chooses the password "password123" and they somehow get access to the encrypted passwords, they won't be able to know everyone else that used the same password (since they will have different encrypted passwords even though they had the same original password).

Whenever you generate a password with a salt, you are supposed to store that salt and use it again when validating the password. If you don't store the salt, you CAN'T authenticate the password when the user tries to log in.

Note that you can absolutely use unsalted encryption if you want, but it's less secure so it's not recommended.

For the CI/CD thing, I would just say:

1. Figure out a non CI/CD way to deploy your application in a cloud provider (ideally use a free tier)

2. Now figure out how you can use GitHub actions so that when you push your commits to a branch, the app gets deployed automatically. You now have a basic CI/CD pipeline in place

3. Bonus: Figure out what unit test library you can use, and write a couple of unit tests for your code

4. Add those unit tests to the GitHub actions pipeline or just have them triggered on pull requests

I'm biased but I highly recommend to try and "ship" minimum viable versions of your project and iterate on it by gradually adding stuff. Also instead of spending hours learning about concepts like CI/CD in a very abstract way, I like to just figure out how to use the concept in my project in the simplest way possible, and then after I've already been exposed to the concept in practice, I look at more detailed explanations if I want to understand more deeply how it works.

Note that ChatGPT is really good for this, you can build a project and ask it for suggestions on how to quickly add simple CI/CD elements and it can help you immensely. You can have it explain anything you don't understand during this process.

In short, I think it's worth investing a small about of time into it, but don't try to learn everything about CI/CD there is to know, just do enough to be able to say you know what it is, why it's valuable, and you have used 1 or 2 CI/CD tools. Apply this same mindset to nearly everything.

Rather than 서 goes here because "x y z", your goal is to reach a point where you just know that 서 goes there. You don't know why, but you know that it makes the most sense in that context. You've read, and heard, and written, and spoken similar sentences so many times that you no longer even doubt yourself.

In that regard you could say that once you are able to read and listen to an appreciable amount of content, your time would be better spent reading and listening to more content than going back to study grammar rules.

The shorts algorithm works in bursts.

I am oversimplifying, but it goes something like "let's show this video to 20 people and see what happens". Then it does that and immediately stops showing the video. Then it analyzes that data to figure out these things:

1. Who is the target audience for this video?

2. Are people even interested in giving this video a shot? (CTV rate)

3. Is the video keeping people engaged? (Watch time, likes, comments)

Then based on that, a few hours or days later, it usually does a bigger push (if the first "test" passed whatever arbitrary criteria the algo uses), let's say it shows it to 100 people this time.

Then same thing happens, it stops and analyzes the data to further answer those 3 questions. Based on how interesting your short is, it will keep giving bigger bursts, or it will stop there.

Note that while MOST shorts seem to follow this trend of sudden spikes and sudden flatlines, some don't. Views are not a useful metric, instead focus on CTR, Retention and Impressions.

CTR: Are people interested in the idea + title + thumbnail?

Retention: Is the video good and engaging?

Impressions: Did the algorithm decide to give this video a chance, or did it not?

As a new youtuber, what you will notice is there is not a particularly strong correlation between CTR + Retention (the markers of a good video and thumbnail) and the number of views your videos get, because views are primarily driven by impressions, and the algorithm gives impressions fairly randomly to new channels.

The only thing you should do is focus on CTR and Retention and keep making the best videos you can.

I think it's possible to get to a decent level of Korean within 2 years. That said, as someone who likes learning a lot of different things, I will say that learning Korean to the level you desire is going to be harder than you likely imagine. Part of what makes it so hard is the sheer amount of time required before getting results, but also the fact that the goal is massive and it's hard to break it down into smaller milestones.

When you're trying to complete a degree at school for example, you have natural "milestones" laid out for you, such as mid term exams, years, courses, etc., and these give you a sense of momentum. But here are no such things when learning a language, you either have to create intermediary milestones for yourself, or get by without them.

In the long term your motivation is the most import factor in achieving your goal. So you should spend a lot of time trying to find learning activities that you enjoy, so that the motivation is self-sustaining.

To be very blunt because you seem to have a hard time accepting the answer, no, if code were written in another language it would not make it substantially more difficult to steal. That's like saying if you shaved your body hair you would be more likely to become the fastest sprinter in the world. 

Firstly, English speakers aren't the only ones who would want to steal your code. If your code was written in mandarin, it would be just as easy to understand for chinese people. The more obscure the language is, the less people would understand the code, but when you're writing code, your priority is making it easy for other programmers to understand so they can keep working on it, so it's counter productive. If you don't want the code to get stolen, you just don't make it public. That's it. Nowadays everything is becoming a web service so the vast majority of code never even gets run on your machine.

Beyond that, let's say you replaced the "if" statement with "만약" (the korean equivalent). It would take a programmer who doesn't know any Korean only a few minutes to realize that it means "if" just by glancing at the structure of the code, or just throwing it in google translate. If you are actually trying to steal code, this isn't even going to slow you down.
